title: Wool and shellfish
hookLine: Marcus strips glamour: a purple robe is sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood (Meditations 6.13)
tomorrow: don't be turned into a Caesar

cards: The sneakers with the right logo. The car in the driveway you slow down to look at. The watch that costs more than a year of groceries.
Some things glow, as if owning one would change who a person is. A new week starts today, and it's called seeing clearly.
It opens with a man who wore the purple of Rome, and who sat down one night and described it in the plainest words he could find.

teach.h: THE COLOR OF POWER WAS PURPLE.
teach.b: In Rome, the color of power was purple. Not crayon purple: a deep dye that came from shellfish and cost a fortune. The emperor wore it.

teach.h: SHEEP'S WOOL DYED WITH SHELLFISH BLOOD.
teach.b: And in Book Six he wrote this about it, in George Long's translation: "this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shell-fish." He does the same with dinner.
A fancy dish of meat is the dead body of a fish, or a bird, or a pig. Fine Italian wine is a little grape juice. He isn't sneering at food or wine.
He's practicing a way of seeing: strip away the glow and look at what a thing actually is. Why would an emperor bother?
Because, Marcus says in the same passage, outward show is one of the great deceivers of the mind. The moment you're most sure a thing is important is the moment it's most likely fooling you.
So he lays such things bare and strips off the words that puff them up. This isn't about despising nice things.
Wool is lovely. Wine can be a gift. It's about taking back the power you've handed to them.
When the car in the driveway turns back into metal, glass and a loan, you're free to like it, or not, without it owning a piece of you. Your line: metal, glass and a loan.

how: Many readers of the Stoics practice this plain description, sometimes called seeing things as they are, and use it on status objects, praise and cravings alike.

o: a public display of feelings you hide inside
the glow that makes a thing seem more than it is
how a person looks to strangers on the street

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood
the dead body of a fish or bird
a great deceiver of the mind

s: Marcus says the purple dye came from shellfish
he calls the robe sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shell-fish.
Marcus says nice things are evil and should be thrown away
he's practicing a way of seeing, not despising wool or wine.
Marcus described his own imperial robe this way
the emperor wore the purple, and still called it wool and shellfish.

games.q: you're the emperor. you're wearing the imperial purple. what do you write in your notebook that night?
o: that it proves how important you are.
that it's sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood.
that you should never wear it again.
games.why: Marcus described it in the plainest words he could, to take back the power the glow had over him.

practice: Let one thing with a glow come to mind, something you own, or want, or envy, and describe it the way Marcus would: what is it made of, where did it come from, what is it underneath the name?
Notice whether the glow changes; you don't have to stop liking it.

wordCard.voice: Outward show. Marcus called it one of the great deceivers of the mind, and stripped his own purple robe down to sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood to see past it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: purple dye, and the shellfish it came from.

carryVoice: Your line: metal, glass and a loan. You are still free to like it, glow or no glow. Day one hundred ninety-nine, in plain words.
